english.html: conspired; of whom (says Horace <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>) there was found but one, Hypermnestra, who spared her consort and husband.

notes.original: Horace aũ liure iij. des Carmes, Ode. xj.
notes.gloss: Una de multis face nuptiali / digna periurum fuit in parentem / splendide mendax et in omne virgo / nobilis aevum — the stanza translated in the text; the print reads nuptali.

english.html: One among many, worthy of the nuptial torch, was splendidly false toward her perjured father, a maiden noble for all time.

And seeing themselves frustrated of their evil intention in this respect, they forge the accusation of the prodigious and horrible crime of which mention has been made; and, this crime being proved, inasmuch as he would deserve also a cruel and monstrous punishment, he required likewise that justice be done him by a like punishment against the calumniators.

It is rightly the punishment of calumniators (that is to say, of those who falsely and with premeditated malice denounce another for some crime) to suffer one like to that which the accused would have to endure, if he were attainted and convicted of the crime imputed to him <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>. A fault certainly inhuman, detestable and great, and one which has at all times been so odious to the good Emperors that they would not allow any colour of right, any abolition public or private, nor even a special permission of the prince, to be able to protect it <sup class="mk" data-key="b2">b2</sup>. And our canonists have justly judged calumniators to be worthy of punishments more cruel and grievous than the accused, if they were convicted of the crimes <sup class="mk" data-key="c2">c2</sup>; and the reason seems to me plain enough: for the other crimes are very often committed without intention and previous deliberation to do wrong, through some light and inconsiderate passion <sup class="mk" data-key="d2">d2</sup>. notes.gloss: The talion against calumnious accusers: the accuser who fails suffers the penalty he sought against the accused.
Cited for the rule that no abolitio, public or private, nor a special licence of the prince, shields a calumniator.

readings.reason: At 5x the fourth sort is a z: flat top bar, diagonal, flat foot bar, no bowl or shoulder; the r of 'tre' and 'par' on the same line is a plain stem with a hooked arm. Wrong sort, transcribed as printed (sic).

At 8x a raised wave-shaped stroke sits centred over the u, the same weight and height as the tilde of 'calũnia' two notes down; not a random blot (a separate speck lies to its right). Printed ũ (wrong sort for 'au'), kept as printed with an uncertain entry.

At 7x the mark over the n is a short dot/tick like the i-dot beside it, not a horizontal bar; 'de' on the same line carries similar specks. No tilde. The point before C is printed '.C.' and normalized per §1.
At 7x the first numeral has three stems (i, i, j with descender) and is as wide as the 'iij' of 'q. iij.' two lines below, twice the 'ij' of 'Paulum. ij.'; viij confirmed (v + three stems).
At 4x the letter has a crossbar on both sides of the stem (italic f, as in 'fallaciter' above), unlike the left-nub ſ of 'accuſa' in note a. 'illec' has a closed-bowl e before the c.

The alphabet restarts at ANNOT. XIX. on this page (first-run b from p034's a, then a b c d). Per §4 and the p031 precedent a same-page restart is keyed a, b2, c2, d2 in body and margin; both readers only renumbered the colliding b. Body markers changed to {c2} and {d2} to match.
